questions.title: Asking for help when you're stuck
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time early in a project when you didn't know how to do something and had to ask a teammate or a more senior developer for help. How did you approach that conversation, and what did you do with the answer afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a behavioral question testing resourcefulness and whether a candidate can ask for help effectively, rather than either staying silently stuck or outsourcing the thinking entirely to someone else. A strong answer shows an attempt was made first -- checking documentation, trying an approach, forming a specific theory -- since teams value someone who tries before asking, but it should also show the candidate didn't stay stuck in silence for an unreasonably long time out of fear of looking unprepared. When actually asking, the question should be specific -- naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down -- rather than a vague 'it's not working,' since a specific question gets a faster and more useful answer. The Action should also cover what happened after getting the answer: not just copying the fix, but understanding why it worked, so the same category of problem doesn't require asking again. Result should state a concrete outcome using STAR -- being unblocked within some stated timeframe, and ideally applying the same concept independently on a later, similar problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell one specific story. Situation: early in my capstone, I couldn't get an OLE DB Destination's fast-load mode to actually speed anything up, and I'd already tried switching the data access mode and rereading the component's tooltips with no luck. Task: I needed to actually understand what I was missing, not just make the error go away. Action: I asked a more experienced developer a specific question -- 'I switched to fast load, but it's still inserting one row at a time based on the execution time, here's what I've already tried' -- rather than just saying it wasn't working. They pointed out I still had the destination's table lock option unchecked, which was serializing the insert behind other activity on the table. Result: once I checked that option, the load time dropped noticeably, and I started checking that same setting by default on every OLE DB Destination I've built since, without needing to ask again. I'd keep the story specific and make sure it lands on that last point -- what I actually learned to do differently afterward.
commonMistakes: Staying stuck in silence for too long before asking, out of fear of looking unprepared
Asking a vague question ('it's not working') instead of naming what was tried and exactly where it broke down
Copying the fix without understanding why it worked, so the same type of problem requires asking again later
Describing a general attitude toward asking for help instead of telling one specific, real story with a stated Result
keyPoints: Show an attempt was made before asking, but don't stay stuck in silence too long either
Ask a specific question naming what was tried and where it broke down
Understand why the answer worked rather than just copying it
Use STAR and state a concrete Result, including what changed afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a reasonable attempt was made before asking for help
Tells a specific, real story using STAR
States a concrete Result, including what was learned or applied afterward

questions.title: Why move from Data Analyst toward BI Engineering
questions.prompt: You've been working as a Data Analyst. What's actually motivating you to grow into a BI Engineer role, and what have you been doing to build toward that?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is specific about what actually changes between the two roles, not just a vague sense that BI Engineer 'sounds like a step up.' A Data Analyst typically works with data and models that already exist, answering business questions and building reports against them; a BI Engineer takes more ownership further upstream -- designing the data model itself, building and maintaining the pipelines and transformations that feed it, and being responsible for a report's reliability and performance, not just its content. A credible motivation names a specific experience that revealed that gap -- for example, repeatedly hitting the limits of what could be fixed inside a single report because the underlying model or data pipeline itself needed to change, and wanting to be the person who can make that change rather than only ever filing a request for someone else to make it. The second half of the answer should show concrete action already taken, not just intention -- specific skills being built (SQL beyond basic querying, data modeling, understanding how data gets from source systems into the model in the first place) rather than a general statement of enthusiasm.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be specific rather than giving the generic 'I want to grow' answer. What actually pushed me toward this was hitting a point, a few times, where a report had a real problem -- slow, or a number that was technically right but the model structure made it clunky to get at -- and the fix wasn't something I could make inside the report itself; it needed a change to the underlying data model or the way data was being loaded in the first place. I kept having to file that as a request for someone else and wait, and I realized I wanted to be the person who could actually make that fix. So I've been deliberately building the skills that sit upstream of where I was working before -- going deeper into SQL past basic querying, actually learning data modeling, understanding what it takes to build and maintain the pipeline that gets data into the model in the first place -- rather than just saying I want the title.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer about wanting to 'grow' without naming the actual difference between the two roles
Describing BI Engineering as just 'more advanced reporting' instead of upstream ownership (modeling, pipelines, reliability)
Stating interest without describing any concrete action already taken toward it
Not having a specific, real experience that motivated the shift
keyPoints: Names the real distinction: Analyst works within an existing model; BI Engineer owns the model/pipeline upstream of it
Motivation should come from a specific, real experience, not a vague sense of career progression
Shows concrete action already taken (specific skills being built), not just stated intention
Avoids treating BI Engineering as simply 'more advanced reporting'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes the two roles
Gives a specific, credible motivation
Describes concrete action already taken

questions.title: Estimating a task in a tool you've never used before
questions.prompt: You're asked to estimate how long it will take to build an Airflow DAG for a new pipeline, but you've never built one from scratch before. How do you approach giving an estimate you can actually stand behind?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer is honest about the actual uncertainty up front rather than quietly guessing a confident-sounding number to avoid looking inexperienced -- saying plainly that this is a new tool and the estimate carries more uncertainty than it would for something already familiar is more useful to whoever's planning around that estimate than false confidence would be. A concrete way to reduce that uncertainty before committing to a number is doing a small, time-boxed spike first -- an hour or two building a trivial two-task DAG -- to get a real feel for how long the unfamiliar parts actually take, rather than estimating purely from reading documentation. The estimate itself is more useful given as a range with the specific uncertainty named (for example, 'two days if this follows the pattern I just tested, possibly four if the actual pipeline's dependencies turn out more complex than my test case'), rather than a single falsely-precise number. It's also worth proactively flagging that the estimate should be revisited once the first real task is actually built, since that's the point where the biggest unknowns in a new tool usually surface.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just make up a confident-sounding number to avoid admitting I haven't built one of these before -- I'd say directly that this is new to me, so my estimate has more uncertainty than it would for something I've done many times. What I'd actually do before giving a number is spend an hour or two building the simplest possible DAG I can -- two tasks, one dependency -- just to get a real feel for the unfamiliar parts instead of estimating off documentation I've only read. Then I'd give a range, not a single number, and say explicitly what it's based on: 'probably two days if this pipeline follows the pattern I just tested, could be closer to four if the real dependencies turn out messier than my test case.' I'd also flag upfront that I'll have a much better estimate once the first real task is built, since that's usually where a new tool's actual surprises show up, not in the planning conversation.
commonMistakes: Giving a falsely confident, single-number estimate to avoid admitting unfamiliarity with the tool
Estimating purely from reading documentation instead of doing a small hands-on spike first
Not naming the specific source of uncertainty, leaving whoever's planning around the estimate with no sense of how solid it actually is
Failing to flag that the estimate should be revisited once real work on the unfamiliar tool actually begins
keyPoints: Be honest about genuine uncertainty rather than giving false confidence to avoid looking inexperienced
A small, time-boxed spike gives a more grounded estimate than reading documentation alone
Give a range with the specific source of uncertainty named, not a single falsely-precise number
Flag that the estimate should be revisited once real work surfaces the tool's actual unknowns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows honesty about uncertainty rather than false confidence
Describes a concrete way to reduce uncertainty before estimating (a spike)
Gives a properly-framed range-based estimate with named assumptions

questions.title: Ramping up on a new tool without slowing the team down
questions.prompt: You join a project that uses Microsoft Fabric, but you've only ever worked in Databricks before. How do you approach getting productive quickly without slowing the team down or pretending to know more than you do?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names what actually transfers and what doesn't, rather than treating the new tool as completely unfamiliar. Delta Lake concepts, Spark notebooks, and medallion-architecture thinking carry over directly from Databricks experience; what's genuinely new is the surrounding platform -- OneLake's shared storage model, Fabric-specific items like Warehouses, Eventstreams, and Direct Lake, and the workspace/capacity administration model. A credible plan: be upfront with the team about exactly which parts are familiar and which are new rather than overstating either; spend focused early time specifically on the unfamiliar Fabric-specific pieces rather than re-learning Spark basics already known; take on a first task that's small and low-risk to build real hands-on familiarity before touching something with higher stakes; and ask specific, well-scoped questions rather than either staying silently stuck or asking a teammate to re-explain something already covered in documentation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by being honest with myself and the team about exactly what transfers. Delta Lake, Spark notebooks, medallion-architecture thinking -- all of that carries straight over from Databricks, so I wouldn't waste ramp-up time relearning things I already know. What's actually new to me is the Fabric-specific layer: OneLake as a shared store, things like Warehouses, Eventstreams, and Direct Lake that don't have a direct Databricks equivalent, and the workspace and capacity administration model. I'd tell the team plainly which parts I'm confident on and which parts I'm not, rather than either overstating my familiarity or being falsely modest about the Spark fundamentals I already have. For a first task, I'd deliberately pick something small and low-stakes to build real hands-on confidence with the Fabric-specific pieces before taking on something where a mistake would actually cost the team time.
commonMistakes: Pretending full familiarity with Fabric-specific concepts just because Databricks experience exists
Spending ramp-up time relearning Spark/Delta basics that already transfer, instead of focusing on what's genuinely new
Taking on a high-stakes task immediately instead of building confidence on something smaller first
Staying quiet about gaps instead of being specific with the team about what's actually unfamiliar
keyPoints: Identify what genuinely transfers (Delta, Spark, medallion thinking) versus what's new (OneLake, Fabric-specific items, workspace model)
Be upfront and specific with the team about the actual gap, not falsely confident or falsely humble
Focus ramp-up time on the genuinely new pieces
Start with a small, low-risk task first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies what transfers vs. what's genuinely new
Describes a credible, specific ramp-up plan
Shows honest communication with the team about the gap

questions.title: Getting paged for a failed pipeline overnight
questions.prompt: You're on call and get paged at 2 AM because last night's pipeline run failed. Walk me through what you'd actually do, from the moment the page comes in to resolving it (or escalating it).
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates triage from full root-cause investigation, since at 2 AM the immediate goal is containing impact, not necessarily a complete fix. First step: acknowledge the page and quickly assess actual severity/impact -- is this pipeline feeding a dashboard a critical stakeholder looks at first thing in the morning, or something with slack before it matters -- since that determines how much urgency is actually warranted right now. Next, check the obvious, fast things first (did a dependency fail, is this a known transient issue with a documented fix, can the job simply be safely retried) before digging deep into logs at 2 AM. If the fix is quick and low-risk (a safe retry, a known workaround), apply it and verify the pipeline completes; if the cause isn't obvious or a quick fix isn't safe to apply alone, escalate rather than guessing at something risky alone in the middle of the night -- escalating when genuinely stuck is the responsible call, not a failure. Either way, follow up the next business day with a clear, written explanation of what happened and what will prevent it from happening again, rather than letting a 2 AM fix go undocumented.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd do is actually acknowledge the page and figure out real impact before doing anything else -- is this feeding something a stakeholder is going to look at first thing this morning, or is there actually some slack before it matters? That changes how urgently I need to act. Then I'd check the fast, obvious things first: did a known dependency fail, is this a transient issue with a documented workaround, can I just safely retry the job -- rather than diving into deep log analysis at 2 AM. If a safe, low-risk fix is available, I'd apply it and then actually verify the pipeline completed successfully before going back to sleep, not just assume the retry worked. If the cause isn't obvious or the fix feels risky to attempt alone in the middle of the night, I'd escalate rather than guess -- that's the responsible call, not a failure on my part. Either way, I'd follow up the next business day with a clear write-up of what happened and what we're doing to prevent it, rather than letting a 2 AM fix just disappear undocumented.
commonMistakes: Treating every page as equally urgent without first assessing actual business impact
Attempting a risky, unfamiliar fix alone at 2 AM instead of escalating when genuinely unsure
Not verifying the pipeline actually completed successfully after a retry before going back to sleep
Letting the incident go undocumented instead of writing a follow-up the next day
keyPoints: Triage severity/impact first, before diving into root cause
Check fast, obvious explanations before deep investigation
Apply a safe fix or escalate rather than guessing at something risky alone
Verify the fix actually worked, and document/follow up afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes triage before deep investigation
Describes a sound decision process for fix vs. escalate
Mentions verification and follow-up documentation
